title: Generate Options & Compare Tradeoffs
summary: Learn how to generate realistic options and compare their benefits, costs, risks, timing, limitations, and consequences before choosing a response.
objectives: Generate more than one reasonable response to a workplace problem.
Compare options using relevant decision criteria.
Explain how tradeoffs affect workplace decisions.

vocab.def: A possible action or approach that could be considered.
The factors used to compare possible choices.
A situation in which gaining one benefit may involve accepting a cost, limitation, or disadvantage elsewhere.
A limit or requirement that restricts which options are realistic.

sections.heading: Do not stop at the first possible solution
sections.body: The first idea may work, but it may not be the strongest option. Generating alternatives can reveal safer, faster, less expensive, more accessible, or more reliable ways to respond.

sections.heading: Use criteria instead of preference alone
sections.body: Useful decision criteria may include safety, quality, cost, time, accessibility, customer impact, policy, available resources, authority, and long-term effects.

sections.heading: Every option can involve tradeoffs
sections.body: One choice may be faster but more expensive. Another may be cheaper but require more time. A third may reduce short-term disruption while creating a larger future burden.

sections.heading: Constraints eliminate unrealistic options
sections.body: An option is not useful if it violates safety requirements, policy, law, authorization, available resources, or other non-negotiable boundaries.

practice.prompt: Two options solve the same problem. One is faster but more expensive. The other costs less but delays the project. What concept are you evaluating?
An option would solve the problem but requires authority you do not have. Should you simply choose it?
practice.answer: No. Authorization is a constraint. The option may need approval, escalation, or a different responsible person.

quiz.question: What is the strongest way to compare possible solutions?
options: Use relevant criteria such as risk, impact, cost, time, and constraints
Choose whichever idea was suggested first
Choose the option you personally prefer
Ignore disadvantages if an option has one major benefit
quiz.answer: Use relevant criteria such as risk, impact, cost, time, and constraints

lab.objective: Generate three options for a simulated workplace problem and compare them using a decision matrix covering benefits, risks, costs, timing, and constraints.

reflectionPrompt: Why can two reasonable people choose different options even when they agree on the facts?
